name: Palouse hills wheat-fallow
region: Inland Pacific Northwest, intermediate rainfall zone
headline: Steep loess hills, winter rain on thawing ground, and a field that sits bare every other year.
story: A 160-acre dryland field west of Colfax alternates winter wheat with a tilled summer fallow to bank moisture. The Palouse has lost topsoil faster than almost anywhere in the country: rain and snowmelt run off frozen, bare slopes. Summers are getting hotter and drier at grain fill. The question is whether a crop can replace the fallow year without starving the wheat of water.

baseline_rotation.name: Winter wheat - summer fallow
baseline_rotation.note: The Cropland Data Layer shows a strict winter wheat - fallow alternation on this field since 2019.

water_context.aquifer: Columbia River Basalt Group (not used for this field)
water_context.in_situ_source: USGS NWIS, Palouse River at Hooper
water_context.note: This is dryland farming. The water that matters is winter precipitation stored in six feet of loess.

winter_wheat.note: Soft white wheat moves by barge to Portland for export; every elevator handles it.

barley.note: Feed barley through local co-ops; malting contracts are limited.

dry_pea.note: Pulse processors in Colfax, Spangle and Moscow.

chickpea.note: The Palouse is the national centre of chickpea processing.

lentil.note: Local processors clean and export lentils.

canola.note: Crush plant at Warden, about 90 minutes away.

reference_yields_basis: Water-unlimited potential for the Palouse. This is a dryland field, so the soil-water balance applies the moisture limit that separates wheat after fallow from wheat after a crop.
